title: Professor Pipkin and the Musical Goose
markdown:
Port Blossom moved the way harbour towns do: by tide, by net, by the slow unfurling of seabirds. Time there was a practical thing. Nets went out on one hour and came back on another, and the lighthouse blink had to mean what the charts said it meant. In a workshop on a cobbled lane that smelled of salt and drying rope, Professor Pipkin lived among timepieces. Gears. Springs. Polished brass. A soft ticking that was less noise than breath. Drawers held screws in sizes that had names only he used. A cracked saucer collected leftover cogs as if they might grow into clocks if left in the sun. He was a mole who could wake a grandfather clock whose pendulum had frozen like a forgotten errand, and who could send a wooden cuckoo back to work with something like joy.

Pip the ginger cat had a velvet cushion of mixed reputation and a degree in sunbeams. He chased dust only when the dust started it. Sometimes he slept on a coil of mainspring and woke looking faintly coiled himself.

"Precision is perfection," Pipkin muttered, which had become the tick of his own worry, "and perfection is all that matters in public." He prided himself on never being wrong where anyone could see. Inspector Hoot was coming: a stern, fair owl, spectacles exact on his beak, a scholar of seconds. The harbour's clocks would be judged. Pipkin's whiskers knew it first.

He pictured gears seizing, pendulums failing, faces in the square turning disappointed. Pip stretched, a ripple of ginger, and purred as if the day were already solved. Then, with a glint that was not helpful and was entirely Pip, he batted a dangling brass weight. The clock hiccupped, recovered, and went on. Life, the cat suggested, was not only synchronicity.

"The Market Square clock must chime at noon," Pipkin said, tightening his tiny spectacles. "The lighthouse to the second. No room." He straightened a waistcoat whose buttons were clock-faces, which would have been funny if he had been in the mood.

They set out, Pip a furry shadow, to put Port Blossom's hours in order.

The Market Square clock had watched generations buy fish and argue about weather. Its face was kind and slightly tea-stained. Pipkin hummed while he worked, a tune that meant either happiness or a screw about to drop. He tightened, listened, tightened again. "Almost there," he whispered to the face. "A little more, and you'll sing."

A large white goose arrived as if the cobbles were a stage and the stage had been poorly managed until now. It puffed. It raised a neck like a question mark of indignation. Market women stepped aside with the politeness reserved for geese and inspectors. It honked, enormous, just as Pipkin touched the escapement.

He jumped. A vital spring leapt from his paw, pinged the tower wall, and vanished into a crack that had been waiting years for a snack. Heat climbed his cheeks and the tips of his ears. For a moment the square's ordinary noises — baskets, gossip, a distant gull — sounded like an audience shifting in their seats. Pip's eyes found the glitter under a leaf. They fitted a replacement, Pipkin's paws not quite as sure as they liked to advertise. The rhythm he wanted — flawless, invisible — had already been interrupted. The goose waddled on, well pleased with the review, leaving a single white feather on the escapement housing as a calling card.

Next, the lighthouse on the headland. Stairs spiraled. Wind had opinions and shared them with anyone climbing. Through the slit windows the sea kept changing its mind about colour. Pip followed with a surprising talent for stone. Pipkin needed a small brass bolt from a narrow ledge, the last honest piece of a kit he had packed twice. It caught the afternoon and winked. The same goose, who appeared to have a diary of Pipkin's appointments, stooped from a glare of sky, snatched the bolt, and headed for the sparkling water with a triumphant noise. An avian bandit. The bolt became a bright comma over the waves, then nothing.

Pipkin's paws made fists. The lighthouse clock ticked on, innocent, missing only the one thing that would keep it honest in a gale. Pip nudged his wrist: another way, then. On the gallery they found a scrap of seagull-discarded shine, a twist of metal that had already lived one life as something else. Pipkin bent it, breathed on it, seated it where the bolt had meant to live. It was not the bolt. It worked. That combination sat in Pipkin poorly, like a joke told in a workshop that preferred silence.

Inspection day arrived sapphire and clear, the kind of sky that makes a harbour look newly washed. Harbour folk filled the square in their better jumpers. Someone had brought a thermos. Children sat on the dry fountain rim. Inspector Hoot landed on the clock tower's platform with official grace, scanned the faces, and nodded once, as if noon itself had filed the correct paperwork. Pipkin took a breath meant to be steady. His waistcoat buttons winked. He told himself the spring was seated, the lighthouse held, the demonstration would be a single clean chime.

The goose came, drawn by an audience.

Pipkin reached to start the town hall demonstration. The goose honked, then offered a flurry of off-key relations of that honk, a family reunion of noise. A baby laughed. A fisherman winced. Inspector Hoot's spectacles flashed.

The clock did not chime. It stuttered. It groaned. What came out was a ghastly braid of bong and honk and whirr and clank, as if several hours had tried to leave through the same door. The sound rattled Pipkin's bones. His vision swam. He mumbled an apology that did not reach the Inspector's ear, and fled, Pip trotting beside him without bounce.

In the workshop the familiar ticking felt like commentary. Each clock, so lately a comfort, seemed to mark the wrongness instead of the minute. He sank onto the worn stool. The air felt thick, salt and oil and leftover pride.

"I'm a failure, Pip."

His hands, which had always known a screw from a wish, looked clumsy. Facing the square again felt like a door that had stuck. The goose's honks stayed in his head, a soundtrack that refused to be filed. He closed his eyes and still saw the Inspector's polite stillness, which is a worse thing for a perfectionist than a frown.

Pip, unbothered in the way of cats who have not been publicly timed, batted a little brass bell on the bench. Ting. Ting. Sweet, clear, not asking permission. A sunbeam found the cushion and stayed, ordinary as bread.

Pipkin watched. Around them, clocks ticked and chimed and whirred, each with its own voice, none of them ashamed of being slightly itself. He thought of the goose not as an enemy but as a musician with no conductor and too much chest. The honk had been rude. It had also been in time, in its own rude way.

"You know, Pip," he said, a spark returning that had nothing to do with shame, "that bird has a rhythm. A flair, even." He stood. The stool creaked as if relieved. "Silence isn't the only kind of right time."

He took the toolbox without the old scramble. Back in the square, faces shifted from pity to curiosity. A few people had not left; disaster is interesting, and so is a mole who comes back. Inspector Hoot's head tilted. Pipkin did not go to the town hall clock. He chose a corner by the fish-stall's shade and built something that looked like a mistake on purpose: gears, yes, but also small trumpets and pipes aimed at the sky, a funnel of bright tin, a spring that had no business being musical and was going to try.

The hour gathered itself. Someone checked a pocket watch and then, catching the mood, put it away. The goose arrived, punctual as a bad habit, chest already filling.

The first honk left the bird. Pipkin's contraption woke with a whir and caught the sound as if it had been invited. The honk came back as notes, odd and rather fine, bouncing off the pipes like a skip across water. The trumpets answered with a lilting line that wove around the call until the square had a tune no one could have scheduled. Not the unblemished chime. Something that made people smile with their mouths closed, then not. A child clapped off the beat, which somehow helped. The goose, surprised to be accompanied, honked again, and the machine, shameless, made a duet of it.

Inspector Hoot's sternness remembered how to grin. His eyebrows rose, feathery and impressed.

"Well," he hooted. "Professor Pipkin. An original symphony."

Pipkin bowed. His whiskers, for once, twitched with a confidence that did not need a perfect second. He had not erased the goose. He had given it a place in the hour. The town hall clock, when it next spoke, still spoke like itself. The extra music had already happened, and the harbour had liked being in on it.

Pip found the warmest stone at Pipkin's feet and began the serious work of napping. A feather — the Market Square calling card, or its cousin — drifted against the toolbox and stayed. Port Blossom kept time after that with a peculiar happy extra in it, the sort of sound a harbour makes when it has decided that a honk, properly caught, can be part of noon.
characters: Professor Pipkin (inventive mole clock repairer), Pip (cat friend)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
